rubric.why: This identifies the quantities used in volume/mass percentage.
rubric.description: States the ratio used to calculate v/m%.
rubric.how: Award for volume of solute divided by mass of solution, multiplied by 100.

rubric.why: The percentage expresses the volume of solute in 100 g of solution.
rubric.description: Explains the meaning of the percentage.
rubric.how: Award for stating the volume of solute present in 100 g of solution.

modelAnswer: Volume/mass percentage (v/m%) is the volume of solute, in millilitres, present in 100 g of solution.
v/m% = (volume of solute in mL ÷ mass of solution in g) × 100.

rubric.why: A pure liquid has a definite boiling point under fixed pressure.
rubric.description: Gives the boiling behaviour of a pure liquid.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a pure liquid boils at a fixed or constant temperature.

rubric.why: A solution generally boils over a range or at a temperature different from that of its pure solvent.
rubric.description: Gives the boiling behaviour used to identify a solution.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a solution has a boiling range or a different/variable boiling point.

modelAnswer: Measure the boiling behaviour under the same pressure.
A pure liquid boils at a fixed, constant temperature, while a solution generally boils over a range or at a different temperature.

rubric.why: Most non-metals are poor conductors of electricity.
rubric.description: Gives a characteristic property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award for identifying their poor electrical conductivity.

rubric.why: Non-metals are generally dull and, when solid, brittle.
rubric.description: Gives another characteristic property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award for one suitable additional physical property.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are elements that generally lack metallic properties.
They are usually poor conductors of heat and electricity, and solid non-metals are generally brittle and non-lustrous.

items.followUp: Write three differences between Dalton’s atomic theory and Thomson’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford allowed electrons to move around the nucleus without specifying fixed energy levels; Bohr proposed fixed permitted orbits.
rubric.description: Contrasts electron paths or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for correctly distinguishing Rutherford’s unrestricted orbits from Bohr’s fixed energy levels/orbits.

rubric.why: In Rutherford’s model orbiting electrons would radiate energy, whereas Bohr’s electrons do not radiate energy in permitted orbits.
rubric.description: Contrasts energy emission in orbits.
rubric.how: Award for the correct comparison of energy radiation.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not account for atomic stability; Bohr’s fixed orbits made atoms stable.
rubric.description: Contrasts the explanation of atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award for stating that Rutherford’s model implied collapse while Bohr’s model explained stability.

rubric.why: Bohr’s model explained the hydrogen line spectrum, unlike Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Contrasts the explanation of atomic spectra.
rubric.how: Award for the correct comparison about the hydrogen spectrum.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons absorb or emit definite amounts of energy when moving between permitted energy levels.
rubric.description: States Bohr’s energy-transition idea.
rubric.how: Award for describing energy absorption or emission during a transition between levels.

modelAnswer: In Rutherford’s theory, electrons revolve around the nucleus without specified fixed energy levels; in Bohr’s theory, electrons occupy fixed permitted orbits or energy levels.
Rutherford’s orbiting electrons would radiate energy continuously; electrons in Bohr’s permitted orbits do not radiate energy.
Rutherford’s model therefore suggested that electrons would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus; Bohr’s model explained the stability of the atom.
Rutherford’s theory could not explain the hydrogen line spectrum; Bohr’s theory explained it.
According to Bohr, electrons absorb or emit definite amounts of energy when they jump between energy levels; Rutherford’s theory did not include these transitions.

items.followUp: Define a mixture and classify mixtures with one example of each type.

rubric.why: A compound consists of elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.
rubric.description: Defines a compound.
rubric.how: Award one mark for stating that it contains two or more elements chemically combined, and one mark for stating that the elements are in a fixed ratio/proportion.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds are one main class of compounds; sodium chloride is an example.
rubric.description: Names the ionic class and/or gives an example.
rubric.how: Award for identifying ionic compounds, preferably with a suitable example.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds are the other main class; water and carbon dioxide are examples.
rubric.description: Names the covalent class and/or gives an example.
rubric.how: Award for identifying covalent compounds, preferably with a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in a fixed proportion by mass.
Compounds are classified as ionic compounds and covalent compounds.
Ionic compounds form by transfer of electrons; sodium chloride (NaCl) is an example.
Covalent compounds form by sharing of electrons; water (H₂O) is an example.
